description: Introduction to Physics - Circuits - Ohm's Law - Q2 (updated to LibreTexts version)
assessments: Questions and Exercises for Sections 9.8 through 9.12
qtext:
To help you develop some intuition for physical quantities in electric circuits, try calculating below quantities to develop some sense of "large" and "small" quantities in electric circuits.

$hintlink[0]

  1. A typical small electronic device (think cell phone or radio) is powered by a battery of a few volts, with circuit elements whose resistances range from 1 kΩ to 100 kΩ. To get a sense of typical amount of current in a situation like this, calculate: amount of current flowing through a resistor of resistance $R1 kΩ powered by a battery of voltage $V1 V.

    The amount of current is $answerbox[0] mA.

  2. A $P2-watt lightbulb operates on household line voltage of $V2 volts and, while it is on, has an effective resistance of $R2 Ω (its resistance is lower when the filament is cold, but as the filament heats up, its resistance increases to $R2 Ω, limiting the amount of current that can flow). Calculate the amount of current flowing through the $P2-watt lightbulb while it is on.

    The amount of current is $answerbox[1] A.

  3. For long segments of wire, it is not unusual to have a resistance as large is 1 Ω. To get a sense of the change of voltage that could occur across a long wire carrying a large amount of current, calculate: voltage change across a wire of resistance $R3 Ω if the wire is carrying a current of $I3 A.

    The voltage change across the wire is $answerbox[2] V.
control: $anstypes=array("number","number","number") $reltolerance=0.02 // slightly higher tolerance for part b rounding $R1=rrand(1,500,1) // resistance in kOhm $V1=rrand(3,5,0.2) // voltage in volts $P2=rrand(40,120,20) // power in W $V2=110 // voltage in volts $R2=prettyreal($V2^2/$P2) // resistance in Ohm $R3=rrand(0.2,1,0.1) // resistance in ohms $I3=rrand(1,10,0.5) // current in amps $answer[0]=$V1/($R1*1e3)*1e3 // current in mA $answer[1]=$V2/$R2 // current in ampere $answer[2]=$I3*$R3 // voltage in volts $hinttext[0]="Review Section 9.9 Ohm's Law. Choose an appropriate form of Ohm's Law for the calculation, `I = V//R`, `R = V//I`, or `V=IR`, and watch out for factors of 10 (watch the metric prefixes)." $hintlink[0]=forminlinebutton("Hint", $hinttext[0])

qtext:
Using the formula for the electric power (`P=IV`), we can develop a sense of electrical quantities for various household appliances. For all questions below, assume household line voltage of 110 volts.

$hintlink[0]

  1. Typical power rating of a microwave (the one appliance most likely to trip the circuit breaker, if you live in an old building) is about 1000 watt. Estimate how much current a microwave of power rating $Power1 watt draws while it is on.

    The $Power1-watt microwave draws current of $answerbox[0] ampere while it is on.

  2. A typical value at which a low-amperage household circuit breaker is set at is 15 ampere. How much power can be drawn from any one wall outlet before the circuit breaker trips?

    Power of $answerbox[1] watt can be drawn from one wall outlet before the circuit breaker set at 15 ampere trips.

  3. An electric stovetop may use anywhere from 1000 W to 3000 W while it is on. Estimate how much current an electric stovetop of power rating $Power2 W draws while it is on.

    The $Power2-W stovetop draws current of $answerbox[2] A while it is on.
